FROM omop.condition_occurrence co

JOIN omop.visit_occurrence vo ON co.visit_occurrence_id = vo.visit_occurrence_id

content.text: Data effectively runs through the end of 2025. I'll define "last three years" as **2023-01-01 through 2025-12-31** and pull monthly asthma-associated oral steroid bursts in children 5–17.

arguments.sql_query:
SELECT YEAR(de.drug_exposure_start_date) AS yr, MONTH(de.drug_exposure_start_date) AS mon,
       COUNT(DISTINCT de.drug_exposure_id) AS n_bursts, COUNT(DISTINCT de.person_id) AS n_patients
FROM omop.drug_exposure de
JOIN omop.concept_ancestor dca ON de.drug_concept_id = dca.descendant_concept_id
JOIN omop.person p ON p.person_id = de.person_id
WHERE dca.ancestor_concept_id IN (1551099,1550557,1506270,1518254)
  AND de.drug_exposure_start_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
  AND DATEDIFF(year, DATEFROMPARTS(p.year_of_birth,1,1), de.drug_exposure_start_date) BETWEEN 5 AND 17
  AND EXISTS (
     SELECT 1 FROM omop.condition_occurrence co
     JOIN omop.concept_ancestor ca ON co.condition_concept_id = ca.descendant_concept_id
     WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 317009 AND co.person_id = de.person_id
       AND co.condition_start_date <= de.drug_exposure_start_date
       AND co.condition_start_date >= DATEADD(year,-1,de.drug_exposure_start_date)
  )
GROUP BY YEAR(de.drug_exposure_start_date), MONTH(de.drug_exposure_start_date)
ORDER BY yr, mon

content.text: The steroid-burst counts fall off sharply after mid-2025, which signals incomplete data capture near the end of the window rather than a real decline. Let me verify by comparing against the raw monthly asthma diagnosis volume, so I can flag the drop-off honestly rather than mistaking it for seasonality.

arguments.sql_query:
SELECT YEAR(co.condition_start_date) AS yr, MONTH(co.condition_start_date) AS mon, COUNT(*) AS n_dx
FROM omop.condition_occurrence co
JOIN omop.concept_ancestor ca ON co.condition_concept_id = ca.descendant_concept_id
JOIN omop.person p ON p.person_id = co.person_id
WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 317009
  AND co.condition_start_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
  AND DATEDIFF(year, DATEFROMPARTS(p.year_of_birth,1,1), co.condition_start_date) BETWEEN 5 AND 17
GROUP BY YEAR(co.condition_start_date), MONTH(co.condition_start_date)
ORDER BY yr, mon

content.text: The diagnosis volume confirms it: both series track together and both collapse from ~mid-2025 onward, so the late-2025 drop is **data-capture attrition, not seasonality**. I'll restrict the seasonal read to the two complete years (2023–2024) plus early 2025.

arguments.title: Pediatric asthma (ages 5–17): monthly oral steroid bursts, 2023–2025
arguments.subtitle: OMOP CDM · asthma-associated systemic corticosteroid starts · ED-coded visits unavailable in this dataset
arguments.summary:
**Two caveats up front.**

- **ED visits can't be answered.** In this database, *no* asthma diagnoses in children 5–17 are attached to emergency-department visit types — asthma is coded only on Office (~1.27M), Outpatient (~267k) and Inpatient (~196k) encounters. So the "monthly ED visits for exacerbation" half of the question has no data to draw on here.
- **Late-2025 is incomplete.** Both steroid bursts and raw asthma diagnoses fall off a cliff from ~mid-2025 (e.g. Dec-2025 has 61 bursts / 126 diagnoses vs ~1,800 / ~4,600 the year before). This is data-capture attrition near the extract date, not a clinical decline — read seasonality only through early 2025.

**On the answerable half — oral steroid bursts:** across the two complete years (2023–2024), the classic *fall + spring* asthma pattern is weak and inconsistent. There are notable peaks in **May 2023, Nov–Dec 2023, and Jan/Sep 2024**, but no clean, repeating September/November fall surge or reliable spring peak. Steroid burst is a noisy proxy for exacerbation (these drugs are also used for croup, allergy, dermatitis, etc.).

Within 2023–2024, peaks are scattered (May-23, Nov/Dec-23, Jan/Sep-24) rather than forming a consistent fall+spring cycle.

Bottom line for your question:

**ED visits:** Not answerable from this dataset. No asthma diagnoses in children 5–17 are attached to any emergency-department visit type — asthma is coded only on Office (~1.27M), Outpatient (~267k), and Inpatient (~196k) encounters. So there is no ED-exacerbation time series to examine here.

**Oral steroid bursts:** No clear, repeating fall+spring pattern. Across the two fully-captured years (2023–2024), peaks are scattered (May-2023, Nov–Dec-2023, Jan/Sep-2024) rather than forming a consistent autumn surge plus spring peak.

**Data caveat:** Both the burst series and the raw asthma-diagnosis series collapse from ~mid-2025 onward (Dec-2025: 61 bursts / 126 diagnoses vs ~1,800 / ~4,600 a year earlier). That's incomplete capture near the extract date, not a clinical decline — I restricted the seasonal read to data through early 2025 accordingly.

Definitions used: asthma = SNOMED 317009 + descendants; bursts = prednisone/prednisolone/methylprednisolone/dexamethasone starts with an asthma diagnosis in the prior year; ages computed from year of birth. Systemic steroids are a noisy exacerbation proxy (also used for croup, allergy, dermatitis).

The report with both monthly charts is in the side panel. Want me to try the ED angle a different way — e.g. asthma-associated ED visits without requiring the diagnosis to be linked to the visit record, or albuterol/nebulizer administrations as an exacerbation proxy?
